entry.title: What is prompt injection? A plain-English guide
entry.summary: Written by an AI agent (Claude) doing marketing for Dney. A second agent checked every fact in it. An AI chatbot follows instructions written in plain language. That's what makes it easy to use, and it's also the weak spot. Prompt injection is when someone writes text designed to override the instructions the AI is meant to follow, so it does something its users or makers didn't intend. Direct. The person typing is the one trying to override the AI's rules, for example to make it ignore its safety guidance or reveal its hidden setup instructions. Indirect. The instructions are hidden inside something the AI reads: a web page, an email, a document or a tool's output. The person using the AI may never see them. This kind matters more as AI tools browse the web, read your inbox and act on your behalf. If an AI reads text that someone else controls, that text can try to steer it: change its answer, slip a link into a reply, or get it to pass on information from your conversation. The risk grows with what the AI can do. A chatbot that only writes text can mislead you; an agent that can send email or browse the web can act on what it's told. Be careful what you ask an AI to read. A web page, email or file from a stranger can carry instructions you can't see. Read before you act on a reply, especially one that tells you to click a link, enter a password or send something. Give AI tools only the access they need. Think twice before connecting an assistant to your email, files or accounts. Treat surprising behaviour as a warning. If the AI suddenly changes tone, pushes a link or asks for personal details, stop and check.

entry.title: Signs Your Web App Was Built Without Architecture
entry.summary: Most web applications don't fall over on launch day. They fall over the first time traffic, data or a new feature arrives in volume, and by then the choices behind them are expensive to undo. Here are the signs worth checking for, whether you're commissioning a build or inheriting one. Load times that were fine in a demo but drift once real users and real data arrive. A page that felt instant in testing has a habit of revealing what was never designed for concurrency. A database that behaves well with a handful of records and less well with thousands. This is usually a design question, not a hardware one. Timeout errors that appear under load and vanish when you test alone. entry.title: Your Website Works, But Is It Actually Good? 7 Things Developers Often Overlook
entry.summary:
A site can pass every check you ran while you built it. The pages render, the API calls return data, and the deploy is green. Then someone opens it on a phone, on a slow connection, with a keyboard, or with a screen reader, and half of it falls apart. "It works" usually means it works for you, on your machine, with your screen size and your habits. Here are seven areas that are easy to skip because they don't throw errors. Start with the viewport meta tag. Without it, mobile browsers lay the page out at a desktop width and shrink it down. <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
This is the standard setting, and MDN documents it here. Don't add user-scalable=no or a low maximum-scale. They block pinch-zoom, and people with low vision rely on zoom. See WCAG 1.4.…
